standard.title: Effects of text structure
standard.description: describe the effects of text structures and language features when responding to and sharing opinions about texts
standard.prior_knowledge: Students discuss how literary devices enhance meaning and shape reader response (AC9E3LE04). They have not yet described the effects of text structures and language features in formal responses to texts.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students can describe how specific text structures and language features produce effects in a literary text, use metalanguage to support their responses, and share opinions about texts by connecting personal response to specific textual evidence.

nodes.label: Identifying structural and language choices
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify specific text structure choices and language features in a literary text and name them using metalanguage.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify one structural feature and one language feature in a literary text and name each using appropriate metalanguage.
nodes.typical_width: Identify a range of structural choices (chapter structure, flashback, circular ending, section breaks) and language features (repetition, figurative language, dialogue, tense choices) across literary texts, naming each with metalanguage.
wider: Compare structural and language feature choices across two texts by different authors writing in the same genre, identifying what each author does differently
Examine how illustrators in picture books use visual structural choices (double-page spreads, white space, sequence) alongside author language choices to create effects
nodes.hinge_reason: Students must have metalanguage to name features before they can describe effects in N2 — without named features, the 'feature to effect' structure in N2 has nothing to anchor to.

response_modes.reason: The metalanguage repertoire for describing structural and language features is built through repeated exposure across varied texts. Students need to encounter features named in context to build a usable vocabulary for literary response.

success_criteria: Can name a structural feature and a language feature in a text using metalanguage
Does not describe effects without naming the specific feature producing them

nodes.label: Describing effects on reader response
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can describe the effect that a specific structural or language choice has on a reader, linking the choice to the response it creates.
nodes.minimum_width: Describe the effect of one identified structural or language feature on the reader, using the structure 'The author uses [feature] to [effect]'.
nodes.typical_width: Describe the effects of a range of structural and language choices across a text, explaining how each choice shapes reader response — creating tension, building empathy, creating humour, establishing mood.
wider: Compare the effects of the same language feature (e.g. repetition) used in two different texts and explain why the effect differs depending on context
Write a short alternative version of a passage using different structural or language choices and describe how the effect changes
nodes.hinge_reason: N3 requires students to support opinions with reference to specific features and their effects. Students who cannot complete the feature→effect link in N2 have nothing to cite in N3.

response_modes.reason: Connecting a specific textual feature to a specific reader effect requires a reasoning scaffold — students often describe their feelings without linking them to what in the text produced the feeling. The 'feature to effect' structure is the scaffold.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The range of effects achievable through different structural and language choices is genuinely rich, and the ability to articulate effect precisely is a high-value literacy capability.
success_criteria: Can name a specific feature and describe the effect it has on the reader
Does not just describe personal feeling — connects feeling to a specific textual choice

nodes.label: Sharing opinions using evidence
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can share an opinion about a text and support it with reference to specific text structures and language features.
nodes.minimum_width: State an opinion about a text and support it with at least one reference to a specific text structure or language feature.
nodes.typical_width: Share a reasoned opinion about a literary text in a discussion or written response, supporting the opinion with multiple references to specific structural and language features and explaining how these features support the view.
wider: Compare personal responses to a text with a peer's, identifying where opinions differ and examining whether different textual features are being prioritised
Respond to a First Nations Australian literary text using metalanguage to describe structural and language features, with attention to how cultural context shapes interpretive choices

response_modes.reason: Sharing a supported opinion integrates identification (node 1) and effect description (node 2) into a coherent reader-response — the full capability the descriptor demands.

success_criteria: Can state a clear opinion about a text and support it with at least one specific textual reference
Does not offer only plot summary — the response engages with how the text is constructed, not just what happens
